31823: Some have compared his name with Vulcan, the Roman god of the forge. Most scholars think the likeness is coincidence.
31825: Placed just before his father's violent song, his metalwork hints that new tools could become weapons.
31826: Strong, skilled and plain-spoken, a craftsman of the forge.
31832: Abraham takes Keturah as a wife. She bears Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah.
31834: Abraham leaves everything to Isaac, gives gifts to his other sons and sends them away eastward.
31835: Keturah is Abraham's later wife, mentioned after Sarah's death. Her six sons become the ancestors of tribes in Arabia, including Midian, the people of Moses' father-in-law Jethro. Genesis calls her a wife, while 1 Chronicles calls her a concubine (a secondary wife). Genesis does not say exactly when the marriage began.
31836: Abraham took Keturah as a wife. She bore six sons, including Midian. 1 Chronicles calls her Abraham's concubine. Abraham gave her sons gifts and sent them east, away from Isaac.
31838: She was a second wife or concubine, and her sons fulfil the promise that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Genesis 17:4).
31840: Some rabbis identify Keturah with Hagar, saying Abraham brought Hagar back after Sarah died.
31841: Keturah is Hagar under another name, called Keturah because her deeds were as pleasant as incense.
31843: Quiet and dignified, the mother of desert peoples.
31851: Laban gives Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant at Rachel's wedding.
31853: Childless Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob so that she can have children 'through' her. Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali, and Rachel names them.
31855: After Rachel dies, Jacob's eldest son Reuben sleeps with Bilhah. Jacob later strips Reuben of his firstborn rank for this (Genesis 49:3-4).
31856: Bilhah was Rachel's maidservant. When Rachel could not have children, she gave Bilhah to Jacob, following a custom known from ancient Near Eastern contracts in which a servant's child counted as the wife's. Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali, ancestors of two tribes. She had little say in what happened to her, and the text tells her story briefly.
31857: Laban gave her to Rachel. Rachel gave her to Jacob as a wife, and she bore Dan and Naphtali. Reuben later slept with her, and Jacob heard of it.
31859: Marriage contracts from Nuzi and elsewhere let a childless wife provide a servant to bear children counted as hers, which explains Rachel's action.
31861: Many note that Bilhah, like Hagar, is used for others' goals and never speaks, and read her story as a reminder of those with little power in the household.
31862: Silent in the text; imagined as patient and watchful, a servant who knows her place is not her own.
31866: Laban gives Zilpah to Leah as her maidservant on Leah's wedding day.
31868: When Leah stops having children she gives Zilpah to Jacob. Zilpah bears Gad and Asher, and Leah names them 'good fortune' and 'happy'.
31869: Zilpah was Leah's maidservant. In the rivalry between Leah and Rachel, Leah gave her to Jacob, and she bore Gad and Asher. Through them she became the mother of two of Israel's twelve tribes.
31870: Laban gave her to Leah. Leah gave her to Jacob, and she bore Gad and Asher. Sixteen of Jacob's descendants who went to Egypt are counted through her.
31872: God builds Israel even through the messy rivalries of Jacob's household; the servant women's sons receive full shares among the tribes.
31873: Rarely heard; imagined as loyal to Leah and quietly proud of her sons.
31878: Leah bears a daughter after her six sons and names her Dinah.
31880: Dinah goes out to visit the women of the land. Shechem, son of the local ruler Hamor, takes her and lies with her by force, then says he loves her and wants to marry her.
31882: Her brothers demand that the men of Shechem be circumcised. While they are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill all the men and take Dinah home. The other sons plunder the city.
31884: Jacob fears revenge from the neighbours. The brothers answer, 'Should he deal with our sister as with a harlot?' On his deathbed Jacob curses Simeon and Levi's anger.
31885: She is listed among Jacob's family who move to Egypt.
31886: Dinah is the only daughter of Jacob whose name is recorded. Her story in Genesis 34 is one of the hardest in the Bible. Shechem, a local prince, takes her by force and then asks to marry her. Her brothers Simeon and Levi trick the men of the city into being circumcised and then kill them all. Dinah herself never speaks, and the text leaves her feelings and later life untold. The chapter raises hard questions about violence against women, revenge, and how far Jacob's family had to go before it would reflect God's ways.
31887: Daughter of Jacob and Leah. Shechem son of Hamor saw her, took her, lay with her and humbled her. He then sought to marry her. Simeon and Levi killed the men of the city and brought her out of Shechem's house. Jacob condemned their violence. She went down to Egypt with the family.
31888: The Hebrew words (took, lay with, humbled) describe rape. The brothers' anger is understandable, but their deceit and mass killing are condemned by Jacob in Genesis 49.
31889: The vocabulary could describe sex without consent of her family rather than physical force. This minority reading is debated and criticised for softening the text.
31890: Some rabbis blamed Dinah for 'going out'. Others reject this, and many modern Jewish and Christian readers see such blame as unjust to the victim.
31892: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15b; Targum on Job 2:9
31893: Silent in Genesis; imagined as a young woman whose story others told for her.
31898: Leah names him Simeon because 'the LORD has heard that I was unloved'.
31899: With Levi he kills the men of Shechem to avenge their sister Dinah.
31901: Joseph, still unrecognised, binds Simeon before his brothers' eyes and keeps him in Egypt until they return with Benjamin.
31903: Jacob calls Simeon and Levi 'instruments of cruelty' and says they will be scattered in Israel.
31905: Simeon's tribe shrinks in the wilderness (from 59,300 to 22,200 fighting men) and receives towns inside Judah's territory, fulfilling Jacob's words.
31906: Simeon is Jacob and Leah's second son. With his brother Levi he took violent revenge on the city of Shechem after their sister Dinah was violated. Years later Joseph chose Simeon to keep as a hostage in Egypt, perhaps because of that violence or because he had a part in selling Joseph. Jacob's last words condemned Simeon's anger, and his tribe did shrink and lose a separate territory. Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 leaves Simeon out altogether.
31907: Second son of Jacob and Leah. He and Levi killed the men of Shechem. Joseph bound him and kept him in Egypt. Jacob cursed his anger and said he would be scattered. His tribe received land inside Judah's inheritance.
31908: Joseph chose Simeon because he had been the one who threw Joseph into the pit or first proposed killing him.
31909: Simeon and Levi show two outcomes of one curse: Levi's scattering became a priestly calling (Exodus 32:26-29), while Simeon's tribe faded into Judah.
31910: The story may reflect the later history of a small tribe that was absorbed by Judah.
31912: Deceit and mass killing at Shechem
31915: Hot-tempered and blunt, quick to defend family honour and slow to count the cost.
31919: Leah 'hires' a night with Jacob from Rachel in exchange for her son's mandrakes. She conceives and names the boy Issachar, 'reward'.
31921: Jacob pictures Issachar as a strong donkey that sees good land and bends his shoulder to forced labour.
31923: Generations later the men of Issachar who join David are praised as 'men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do'.
31924: Issachar is Jacob and Leah's fifth son, born after a strange bargain between Leah and Rachel over mandrakes, a plant thought to help fertility. His name plays on the Hebrew word for 'hire' or 'reward'. His tribe settled in the fertile Jezreel Valley. Jacob's blessing pictures them as hardworking but willing to serve others for the sake of good land. Later, the men of Issachar were praised for wisdom about the times.
31925: Fifth son of Jacob and Leah. Jacob compared him to a strong donkey who submits to labour. The tribe sent princes with Deborah (Judges 5:15), and its men understood the times (1 Chronicles 12:32).
31926: Steady and hardworking, a man who prefers a quiet field to a fight.
31931: Leah names him Zebulun, hoping that now her husband will 'dwell with' or honour her.
31932: Jacob says Zebulun will live by the seashore and be a haven for ships, with his border toward Sidon.
31934: Zebulun's men answer Barak's call and are praised in Deborah's song as a people who risked their lives to the death.
31936: Isaiah promises that the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, once humbled, will see a great light. Matthew sees this fulfilled when Jesus settles in Capernaum.
31937: Zebulun is Jacob and Leah's sixth son. His tribe settled in lower Galilee, the hill country around Nazareth. Zebulun's warriors fought bravely with Deborah and Barak. Isaiah later promised that this northern region, the first to suffer Assyrian invasion, would see a great light. Matthew applies that promise to Jesus' ministry in Galilee.
31938: Sixth son of Jacob and Leah. Jacob linked him with the sea and trade. His tribe fought under Barak and later sent 50,000 skilled soldiers to David (1 Chronicles 12:33). Isaiah and Matthew name his land as a place of coming light.
31939: Outgoing and adventurous, looking toward the sea routes and the wider world.
31943: Leah's maidservant Zilpah bears him, and Leah says, 'Good fortune has come!'
31944: In a play on his name, Jacob says raiders will raid Gad, but Gad will raid at their heels.
31946: Gad's tribe, rich in livestock, asks for the grazing land of Gilead. Moses agrees on condition that they help conquer Canaan first.
31948: Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh build an altar by the Jordan. The other tribes nearly go to war until they learn it is a witness of shared faith, not a rival altar.
31949: Gad is Jacob's son by Zilpah, Leah's servant. His name means 'good fortune'. His tribe raised livestock and settled in Gilead, east of the Jordan, on the exposed frontier with Ammon and the desert peoples. Gadites became known as tough fighters, described as having 'faces like lions' (1 Chronicles 12:8).
31950: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, full brother of Asher. Jacob foresaw Gad being attacked and striking back. His tribe received land east of the Jordan after promising to fight alongside the others.
31951: Brisk and battle-ready, a frontiersman used to defending his herds.
31954: Leah calls him Asher: 'Happy am I, for women will call me blessed.'
31955: Jacob promises Asher rich food fit for kings.
31957: Asher fails to drive out the Canaanites of Acco and Sidon, and stays by the coast instead of joining Deborah's battle.
31958: Anna of the tribe of Asher
31959: The prophetess Anna, who welcomes the infant Jesus in the temple, is from Asher.
31960: Asher is Jacob's second son by Zilpah. His name means 'happy'. His tribe received fertile land along the coast north of Mount Carmel, toward Tyre and Sidon, famous for olive oil. Asher did not drive out the coastal Canaanites and lived among them. Centuries later the elderly prophetess Anna, from Asher, was among the first to recognise the child Jesus.
31961: Son of Jacob and Zilpah. Jacob and Moses blessed him with rich food and oil. His tribe lived among the Canaanites on the coast. Anna the prophetess was of his tribe.
31962: Cheerful and prosperous, fond of good food and good company.
31966: Rachel names Bilhah's second son Naphtali: 'With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.'
31967: Jacob calls Naphtali a doe let loose who gives beautiful words.
31969: Barak, Deborah's general, comes from Kedesh in Naphtali, and Naphtali's men risk their lives in battle.
31971: The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser takes the land of Naphtali and deports its people.
31973: Isaiah's promise of light to Zebulun and Naphtali is applied by Matthew to Jesus' ministry around the Sea of Galilee.
31974: Naphtali is Jacob's second son by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. Rachel named him after her 'wrestling' with her sister Leah. His tribe held the hills west of the Sea of Galilee. Barak came from Naphtali, and the tribe was among the first deported by Assyria. Jesus' Galilean ministry took place largely in this land, which Matthew links to Isaiah's promise of light.
31975: Son of Jacob and Bilhah, brother of Dan. Jacob compared him to a free-running doe. His tribe settled in upper Galilee, fought with Barak, and was taken into exile by Assyria.
31976: Quick and graceful, with a way with words.
31979: Rachel says, 'God has judged me and heard my voice,' and names Bilhah's son Dan.
31980: Jacob says Dan will judge his people, but also calls him a snake by the road that bites the horse's heels.
31982: Pushed out of its coastal land, the tribe of Dan seizes the quiet town of Laish in the far north, renames it Dan, and sets up Micah's stolen idol there.
31984: Jeroboam I places one of his two golden calves at Dan, making it a centre of false worship.
31985: Dan is Jacob's first son by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. His name means 'judge'. The tribe first received land near the coast, where Samson the Danite later lived, but it was pushed into the hills and migrated to the far north. There it set up a stolen idol and later hosted one of Jeroboam's golden calves. 'From Dan to Beersheba' became a phrase for the whole land. Dan is left out of the list of tribes in Revelation 7, which has led to much speculation.
31986: Son of Jacob and Bilhah. Jacob called him a judge and a snake by the road. His tribe moved north to Laish and worshipped Micah's idol there. Samson was a Danite (Judges 13:2).
31988: Dan's absence from Revelation 7 and Jacob's 'snake' image led some to say the Antichrist would come from Dan.
31990: Dan is left out of Revelation 7 because of the tribe's early idolatry, or simply to keep the number at twelve once Joseph's sons are counted. The Antichrist idea is speculative.
31991: Shrewd and watchful, quick to strike when cornered.
31993: Israel (born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother)
31996: Joseph's second son by Asenath, born before the famine. Joseph names him Ephraim: 'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.'
31998: Jacob claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon. This gives Joseph a double share among the tribes.
32000: Jacob crosses his arms to put his right hand on the younger Ephraim. When Joseph objects, Jacob says the younger will be greater.
32002: Chronicles records that men of Gath killed some of Ephraim's sons. He mourns many days, then names a newborn son Beriah, 'in misfortune'.
32004: Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor, is from Ephraim's line.
32005: Ephraim is Joseph's younger son, born in Egypt to Joseph's Egyptian wife Asenath. Jacob adopted him and his brother Manasseh as his own sons, and in blessing them he deliberately put the younger Ephraim first. This pattern of the younger son being chosen runs right through Genesis (Isaac, Jacob, Joseph). Ephraim's tribe became the most powerful in the north. It produced Joshua, held the sanctuary at Shiloh, and its name became a poetic name for the whole northern kingdom of Israel, as in Hosea's 'How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?'
32006: Second son of Joseph and Asenath, born in Egypt. Jacob adopted him and blessed him above his older brother. Joseph lived to see Ephraim's children 'of the third generation' (Genesis 50:23). His tribe was large and proud, and the prophets used 'Ephraim' for the northern kingdom.
32007: The crossed hands show that God's choice does not follow human rank or birth order. Some see the half-Egyptian Ephraim as an early sign of God's blessing reaching the nations.
32008: To this day parents bless sons on the Sabbath with Jacob's words: 'God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh' (Genesis 48:20).
32009: The story explains why the tribe of Ephraim came to dominate the north, and the later rivalry between Ephraim and Judah.
32010: Confident and favoured, aware that he received a blessing he did not earn by birth.
32014: Joseph names him Manasseh: 'God has made me forget all my toil and all my father's house.'
32016: Although he is the firstborn, Jacob puts his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh, saying both will be great but the younger greater.
32018: Joseph lives to see the children of Manasseh's son Machir, who are 'brought up upon Joseph's knees'.
32019: A tribe on both sides of the Jordan
32020: Half the tribe settles in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan; the other half settles west of the Jordan around Shechem.
32021: Manasseh is Joseph's firstborn son, born in Egypt to Asenath. His name expresses Joseph's relief that God had helped him 'forget' his suffering. Jacob adopted him along with Ephraim but gave Ephraim the greater blessing. Manasseh's descendants became a large tribe split across both sides of the Jordan. Gideon came from Manasseh, as did the daughters of Zelophehad, who won inheritance rights for women.
32022: Firstborn of Joseph and Asenath. Adopted by Jacob and blessed second. His son was Machir, father of Gilead. His tribe was divided east and west of the Jordan. 1 Chronicles 7:14 mentions an Aramean concubine as a mother in his household.
32023: Ephraim and Manasseh are held up as brothers without rivalry, in contrast to Cain and Abel or Jacob and Esau, which is why parents bless children in their names.
32024: He is often used as an example of accepting God's choice of another without bitterness.
32025: Even-tempered and gracious, a firstborn content to share the blessing.
32031: The Midianite or Ishmaelite traders sell Joseph to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
32033: Seeing that the LORD makes everything Joseph does succeed, Potiphar puts him over his whole household. God blesses the household for Joseph's sake.
32035: Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce Joseph. When he refuses, she accuses him of attempted rape. Potiphar, angry, puts Joseph in the king's prison.
32036: Potiphar was an Egyptian official, called 'captain of the guard', who bought Joseph as a slave. He trusted Joseph with his whole household because he saw that God was with him. After his wife falsely accused Joseph, Potiphar had him imprisoned. Some readers notice that he sent Joseph to prison rather than having him killed, which may hint that he doubted his wife's story. He is a different man from Potipherah, Asenath's father.
32037: An officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. He bought Joseph, prospered because of him, put him over his house, and then imprisoned him after his wife's accusation. The Hebrew word for 'officer' (saris) can also mean 'eunuch'.
32039: A slave accused of attacking his master's wife would normally be executed, so the prison sentence suggests Potiphar was not fully convinced.
32041: The text says only that he was angry. Putting Joseph in the royal prison may simply reflect his rank and access to that prison.
32042: Formal, busy and practical, a high official who trusts results.
32045: Egyptian, probably 'belonging to the goddess Neith'
32048: Pharaoh gives Joseph a new Egyptian name and marries him to Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On (Heliopolis).
32050: Before the famine she bears Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
32051: Asenath was an Egyptian woman, the daughter of a priest of the sun god at On (Heliopolis), whom Pharaoh gave to Joseph as his wife. She became the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim, and so of two of Israel's tribes. Genesis does not say whether she came to worship Israel's God. Later Jewish writers were troubled that a patriarch married a priest's daughter, and they told stories to explain it.
32052: Daughter of Potipherah, priest of On. Pharaoh gave her to Joseph. She bore Manasseh and Ephraim in Egypt.
32054: Asenath was actually Dinah's daughter, carried to Egypt and raised by Potipherah, so Joseph did not marry outside the family.
32056: Her marriage to Joseph is a picture of the church, drawn from the nations and joined to Christ.
32057: In the novel *Joseph and Aseneth*, Aseneth rejects her idols, repents, and is transformed by an angel before marrying Joseph.
32058: *Joseph and Aseneth* (Jewish or Christian romance, c. 1st century BC to 2nd century AD)
32059: Dignified and reserved, a priest's daughter between two worlds.
32065: Tamar bears twins. Zerah's hand comes out first and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, but Perez is born first. 'How hast thou broken forth?' she says, and he is named Perez.
32066: He and his sons Hezron and Hamul are listed among Jacob's family going to Egypt.
32068: The elders of Bethlehem bless Boaz: 'Let thy house be like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah.'
32069: Perez is the son of Judah and Tamar, born after Tamar disguised herself to secure the child Judah had wrongly denied her. He is a twin who 'broke through' ahead of his brother Zerah. Through Perez the line of Judah runs to Boaz, David and, in Matthew and Luke, to Jesus. His clan became the leading family of Judah.
32070: Twin son of Judah and Tamar, born ahead of Zerah. Father of Hezron and Hamul. Named in the genealogies of Ruth, Chronicles, Matthew and Luke.
32071: Matthew names Tamar in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:3). Perez's birth from a scandalous situation shows God working his purposes through flawed people.
32072: The Messiah is to come from Perez's line, through David; some rabbis call the Messiah 'son of Perez'.
32073: Bold and pushing forward, a firstborn by his own energy.
32078: He is listed among the grandsons of Judah who go to Egypt with Jacob.
32080: His sons Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai (Caleb) head the major clans of Judah.
32082: At sixty he marries a daughter of Machir son of Manasseh. Their descendants include Jair, who held twenty-three towns in Gilead.
32083: Hezron is Perez's son and Judah's grandson, one of the family who went down to Egypt. In Chronicles he is the root of Judah's main clans: through Ram comes David's line, and through Chelubai (Caleb) comes the family of Hur and Bezalel. A late marriage to a daughter of Machir links Judah's family with the tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan.
32084: Son of Perez. Father of Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai, and by a later marriage of Segub. Named in the genealogies of Ruth, Matthew and Luke.
32085: A patriarch of many clans, proud of his growing family.
32090: Hezron fathers Ram, and Ram fathers Amminadab.
32091: Ram is Hezron's son and Amminadab's father. Nothing is told about him except his place in the line from Judah to David. He probably lived during Israel's years in Egypt. Some manuscripts of Luke have two different names (Admin and Arni) where the KJV has Aram.
32092: Son of Hezron and father of Amminadab. Listed in Ruth, Chronicles and Matthew.
